[THOUGHT] The infant is 3 months old with several weeks of a non‑itchy, red/scaly rash localized to the scalp and forehead. The age, chronicity, scalp-predominant distribution, absence of systemic symptoms or notable discomfort, and lack of prominent pruritus strongly favor infantile seborrheic dermatitis ("cradle cap"). Typical cradle cap presents in the first months of life with greasy/yellowish scales or crusts on the scalp and sometimes extends to the forehead/eyebrows/behind the ears; it is usually not very pruritic and the infant remains well. Atopic dermatitis would more commonly be itchy and involve the cheeks or flexural areas in infants and often has a stronger family history; tinea capitis, impetigo, or psoriasis are less likely given the presentation and course. Although the caregivers did not describe the exact character of the scales, the overall pattern makes seborrheic dermatitis the most probable diagnosis.

[THOUGHT] The infant is 3 months old with several weeks of a non‑itchy, red/scaly rash localized to the scalp and forehead. The age, chronicity, scalp-predominant distribution, absence of systemic symptoms or notable discomfort, and lack of prominent pruritus strongly favor infantile seborrheic dermatitis ("cradle cap"). Typical cradle cap presents in the first months of life with greasy/yellowish scales or crusts on the scalp and sometimes extends to the forehead/eyebrows/behind the ears; it is usually not very pruritic and the infant remains well.
